title: Data Modeling
description: Design schemas that balance performance, flexibility, and data integrity. Explore normalization, denormalization, indexing, ACID versus BASE, and when to use multiple data stores.

data.text: Data modeling is the process of organizing how information is stored, accessed, and related. A poor data model makes every query slow, every migration painful, and every feature expensive. A good data model lets your system grow gracefully.
As a senior engineer, you will choose between multiple database types, decide how much to duplicate data, and design schemas that serve both current needs and future growth.

Normalization removes duplicate data by splitting it across related tables. Denormalization intentionally duplicates data to speed up reads. Both are valid strategies. The choice depends on whether your workload is read-heavy, write-heavy, or balanced.

cards.title: Normalized Schema
cards.description: Data is split into multiple related tables with minimal duplication.
pros: Writes are fast — only one place to update
Data integrity is easy to maintain
cons: Reads require JOINs, which can be slow
Complex queries are harder to write

cards.title: Denormalized Schema
cards.description: Data is duplicated across tables to reduce JOINs and speed up reads.
pros: Reads are fast — no JOINs needed
cons: Writes are slower — multiple places to update

data.text: Indexes are lookup tables that let the database find rows faster — like the index at the back of a book. Without indexes, every query scans the entire table. With too many indexes, every write becomes slower because the database must update every index.

data.title: Indexing Best Practices
items: Index columns used in WHERE, JOIN, and ORDER BY clauses
Use composite indexes for queries that filter on multiple columns
Avoid indexing low-cardinality columns like gender or boolean flags
Monitor index usage and remove indexes that are never used
Consider covering indexes for frequently accessed data

data.text: ACID guarantees atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability. It is the standard for relational databases like PostgreSQL. BASE stands for Basically Available, Soft state, and Eventually consistent. It is the model used by many NoSQL databases.

rows: Eventual consistency — data converges over time

data.text: Polyglot persistence means using multiple database types in one system. A typical modern application might use PostgreSQL for transactional data, Redis for caching, Elasticsearch for search, and S3 for file storage. Each tool solves a specific problem better than a single database could.

data.title: Pro Tip
data.text: Start with one database type. Add a second only when you have a clear, measured reason. Every new database adds operational complexity, a new failure mode, and data synchronization challenges.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Normalize for write-heavy workloads; denormalize for read-heavy workloads
Index strategically — every index speeds up reads but slows down writes
ACID guarantees strong consistency; BASE prioritizes availability and partition tolerance
Polyglot persistence solves specific problems better than a single database type
Always validate schema changes with representative queries before deployment
data.takeaway: Data modeling is about trade-offs. There is no universal right answer — only the answer that fits your workload.

items.question: Should I always normalize my database?
items.answer: Not always. Normalization is great for transactional systems where data accuracy matters most. For reporting or analytics, denormalization often produces better performance.

items.question: How do I know if I need a composite index?
items.answer: Look at your slow query log. If the same query filters on columns A, B, and C together, a composite index on (A, B, C) is usually the fastest fix.

items.question: What is the biggest mistake in data modeling?
items.answer: Designing for unknown future requirements. It leads to over-engineering. Model for what you know today, and design migrations for what you might need tomorrow.

data.title: Design a Data Model for a Task Manager
data.description: Design a database schema for a team task manager. Users create projects, add tasks to projects, assign tasks to team members, and comment on tasks. Include tables, relationships, indexes, and explain your normalization choices.
data.expectedOutcome: A schema diagram or table listing with primary keys, foreign keys, indexes, and a brief justification for normalization level.
